Q: How to unnest a list-column as new rows in pre-existing columns? A:

You can unnest and preserve the row_id. Then set ord = 1 for the unnested, and ord = 0 for the normal columns, then order by both. For 500k rows, this takes ~80 ms.

library(tibble)

ex = tibble(
  x = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  y = 1:5,
  z = list(tibble(x = "A2", y = 1.5), NA, NA, tibble(x = "D2", y =  4.5), NA)
)

ex2 <- ex[rep(1:5, 10^5),]

f <- function(ex) {
  is_nested <- !is.na(ex$z)
  unnested <- cbind(row_id = which(is_nested), collapse::rowbind(ex$z[is_nested]), ord = 1L)
  main  <- cbind(row_id = seq_len(nrow(ex)), ex[c("x", "y")], ord = 0L)
  collapse::roworder(collapse::rowbind(main, unnested), row_id, ord)[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE] |> 
    tibble::tibble()
}

f(ex)
# # A tibble: 7 × 2
# x         y
# <chr>   <dbl>
# 1 A       1  
# 2 A2      1.5
# 3 B       2  
# 4 C       3  
# 5 D       4  
# 6 D2      4.5
# 7 E       5  

bench::mark(f(ex2), min_iterations = 50)
# A tibble: 1 × 13
# expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc total_time result                 memory     time            gc      
# <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>   <bch:tm> <list>                 <list>     <list>          <list>  
# 1 f(ex2)     76.9ms   77.6ms      12.9    59.1MB     41.9    12    39      931ms <tibble [700,000 × 2]> <Rprofmem> <bench_tm [50]> <tibble>

Shorter version if interleaving is not needed

na.omit(collapse::rowbind(ex[-3], collapse::unlist2d(ex[[3]])[c("x", "y")]))

Shorter version if interleaving is needed

this uses Thomas' great interleaving ordering trick. But this is 18 times slower than my initial function f().

na.omit(collapse::ss(collapse::rowbind(ex[-3], collapse::unlist2d(ex[[3]])[c("x", "y")]),collapse::radixorder(rep(seq_len(nrow(ex)), 2))))

Benchmark - 50k rows

N = 10^4

ex = tibble::tibble(
  x = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  y = 1:5,
  z = list(tibble::tibble(x = "A2", y = 1.5), NA, NA, tibble::tibble(x = "D2", y =  4.5), NA)
)[rep(1:5, N),]


library(data.table)

f_ord_sort = \(ex) {is_nested <- !is.na(ex$z);  unnested <- cbind(row_id = which(is_nested), collapse::rowbind(ex$z[is_nested]), ord = 1L); main  <- cbind(row_id = seq_len(nrow(ex)), ex[c("x", "y")], ord = 0L); collapse::roworder(collapse::rowbind(main, unnested), row_id, ord)[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE]}
f_ord_ord  = \(ex) na.omit(collapse::ss(collapse::rowbind(ex[-3], collapse::unlist2d(ex[[3]])[c("x", "y")]),collapse::radixorder(rep(seq_len(nrow(ex)), 2))))
thomas     = \(ex) { id <- 1:nrow(ex); do.call(rbind,c(split(ex[-3],id), setNames(ex[["z"]],id))[order(rep(id,2))]) |> na.omit()}
i_o        = \(ex) { ex <- as.data.table(ex); ex[, id := .I] |> setkey(id); datatable_solution <- \(){list(ex[, .(id, x, y)], ex[!is.na(z), rbindlist(z), by = "id"]) |> rbindlist() |>_[order(id), -c("id")]}}
m          = \(ex) ex |> dplyr::mutate(z = purrr::map(z, \(z) if (is.data.frame(z)) z else NULL)) |> purrr::pmap_dfr(\(x, y, z) dplyr::bind_rows(tibble::tibble(x, y), z))
rui_thomas = \(ex) {id <- 1:nrow(ex); rbind(ex[-3], do.call(rbind, ex[[3]]))[order(rep(id,2)), ] |> na.omit()}

bm <- bench::mark(
  f_ord_sort(ex),
  f_ord_ord(ex),
  thomas(ex), 
  i_o(ex), 
  m(ex), 
  rui_thomas(ex),
  check = FALSE,
  min_time = 10
) |> sort_by(~ median)

bm

Q: Why Bionic C runtime library in Android does not support "%n" format in printf function? A:

Android leaves out the printf %n "formatter" because it's a security risk. If someone can supply a printf format string and arguments to code they're trying to compromise, they can write four bytes of their (somewhat constrained) choice into memory at any address.

This isn't just theory, it has been exploited many times, and is rarely useful. Leaving it out of Bionic was a sound decision; I've been looking for ways to prevent it being used on other platforms.

Addendum:

Blocking it on GlibC platforms looks possible with a little ingenuity: you use register_printf_function() to redefine the formatter for the %n conversion to something that throws an error.

On Windows, %n gives an invalid parameter error by default. You can use _set_printf_count_output( 1) to enable it, and _set_printf_count_output( 0) to disable it.

On Apple platforms, the printf(3) manpage with Xcode 26 is from 2009. They don't provide a way to turn off %n in that, but they have provided a safety feature.

%n only works on Apple if the format string containing it is in unwritable memory. If it is in writable memory, printf() calls abort() rather than process the format string. The practical effect of this is that you can use %n in string literals in your source code, but not in format strings you create at runtime. .

An intruder trying to exploit the feature on Apple has a fairly difficult job: they need to call mprotect(2) to make the memory holding their format string un-writable before they can use it. It's going to be easier for them to use it for a denial-of-service attack.

While writing code to check out the Apple arrangement, I spotted a not-completely-crazy use case for %n:

  • sprintf( editor_buffer[linenumber].text, "%s%n%, string_with_processed_text, &(editor_buffer[linenumber].length)); for maintaining lengths of lines in an editor.

Q: Update database schema from entities (without using entity framework migration) in .net core A:

This can be done with a little effort using EF Core's internal classes. This is likely much easier than when the question was first asked.

Based on the steps for 'scaffolding' a database. You need to;

  1. Use IDatabaseModelFactory.Create() to read the schema of the database.

  2. Use IScaffoldingModelFactory.Create() to convert the schema into an IModel.

Based on the process for generating a new migration;

  1. Use IMigrationsModelDiffer.GetDifferences() to compare this database model against your dbContext.Model to build a list of MigrationOperation.

And based on the process for generating migration sql;

  1. use IMigrationsSqlGenerator.Generate() to convert these migration operations into sql statements.

Given the age of the question, I'll leave the rest of the details up to anyone who still requires a tool like this.

To close the loop, you'll probably want to run the rest of the 'scaffolding' process to save your new model as source code. So you can repeat this process again later.
